props.title: Straight Time
props.initialSlug: Ex-con's struggle between reform and crime pull

sections.content: Straight Time stands as one of the grittiest and most authentic crime dramas of the 1970s, anchored by Dustin Hoffman's raw performance as ex-con Max Dembo. The film ruthlessly deconstructs the "going straight" narrative, showing how systemic barriers and societal prejudices make rehabilitation nearly impossible. Director Ulu Grosbard and Hoffman (who initially directed portions before stepping back) craft a Los Angeles rarely seen on screen - not the glitzy Hollywood hills but the dusty San Fernando Valley streets where desperate men make desperate choices.

sections.content: The film shares DNA with other character-driven crime studies of the era like The Friends of Eddie Coyle (1973) and Mean Streets (1973), where criminal life isn't glamorized but depicted as a grinding, anxiety-filled existence. Hoffman's Max Dembo ranks alongside Thief (1981) and Taxi Driver (1976) in showing how Vietnam-era alienation and institutional failure created a generation of men unable to reintegrate into society.

What sets Straight Time apart is its attention to procedural detail and crushing bureaucracy. The scenes between Hoffman and M. Emmet Walsh's vindictive parole officer expose how the system is designed for failure rather than rehabilitation. This influenced later prison/parole films like American Me (1992) and 25th Hour (2002), which similarly examine how the justice system perpetuates cycles of crime. sections.content: Like Blue Collar (1978) and The Killing of a Chinese Bookie (1976), Straight Time presents crime as just another desperate way to make a living in a system rigged against working people. The robbery sequences aren't slick heist movie setpieces but tense, messy affairs closer to workplace accidents than glamorous scores. This influenced later films like Out of Sight (1998) and Hell or High Water (2016) in their portrayal of crime as economic survival.
